extracted.intended_audience: lawmakers, political reformers, students of government and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and practical criteria for structuring national and local representative institutions, judicial and civil service appointment/tenure, and electoral constituencies. Focuses on reducing deadlock, securing impartial administration, and promoting civic education through local bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive independence balanced with parliamentary accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The head of the administration should not be so completely dependent on the votes of a representative assembly that deadlock or continual subservience results; options include appointment by Parliament for a fixed term or giving the executive the power to dissolve the House and appeal to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the executive could only be removed by Parliament it should, where practicable, have the power to dissolve Parliament so that instead of being turned out by a hostile vote it faces resignation or dissolution. This avoids prolonged deadlock that could invite coups or mutual paralysis and does much to preserve functional government where mutual forbearance cannot be relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary power to remove a potentially usurping chief magistrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there exists a risk that the chief magistrate could usurp sovereign power (due to concentrated authority and weak public attachment to free institutions), the Parliament must be able, by a single vote, to reduce the magistrate to private station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where peril of subversion exists, only a first magistrate who is effectively removable by Parliament should be admissible; otherwise constitutional dependence offers weak protection against usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence from popular election
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial officers should not be appointed or made removable by popular election; the popular judgment is poorly fitted to estimate their special and professional qualifications and popular responsibility risks politicizing decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although irremovability has evils, the peculiar position of judges makes irresponsibility (except to conscience and public opinion) less likely to pervert conduct than responsibility to the executive or suffrages. Public control over justice is best exercised by juries, not by electing judges. Periodic popular re-election of judges is deemed highly dangerous and likely to make judges decide for public applause rather than justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial tenure and removal only for serious proven misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges and permanent public servants should not be liable to removal except for positive, proved, and serious misconduct (not merely for political reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irremovability is an evil in itself, but for judges the safeguards of impartiality and freedom from political connection often outweigh the disadvantages; removal should be limited to conduct that makes them amenable to criminal or similar accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: First appointments to public service by open competitive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial appointments to the permanent public service should be determined by public competitive examinations administered by persons not engaged in politics and of high standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examinations should be competitive (not mere pass exams) and appointments given to the most successful candidates, with ranking by merit. Examinations should test liberal education subjects likely to indicate general mental cultivation; allowing marks for other useful subjects is acceptable but lowering standards or political nomination undermines public service quality and educational incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examinations must be competitive and merit-ranked
rubrics_metrics.description: Examinations should be competitive so that candidates are classed in order of merit and appointments go to those who most distinguish themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere pass examination only excludes absolute dunces and invites lowering standards through indulgence. Competitive exams stimulate educational institutions and raise the quality of candidates nationwide; relaxing standards creates precedents that reduce attainment over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequent promotion by mixed seniority-and-selection system
rubrics_metrics.description: After initial competitive appointment, promotions should generally follow a mixed system: routine duties advance by seniority, while positions requiring special capacity or trust are filled by selection at the discretion of the chief of the office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection will generally be honest if initial appointments were by open competition because the office will contain competent persons not chosen by patronage; chiefs are incentivized to appoint the most useful subordinates who help maintain the office's reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local affairs should be handled by local representative bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: A large portion of public business cannot be well done centrally; local administration, including watching local officers, providing or withholding supplies, and managing local taxation, should rest with people of the locality via representative bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local functions are chief instruments of public education and civic cultivation. Administration by the assembled people is inadmissible; representative local bodies (municipal, provincial) are fundamental institutions of free government. Local bodies also provide practical opportunities for citizens to act, not merely think.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local electoral franchise tied to contribution to local rates
rubrics_metrics.description: The electoral franchise for local bodies should vest in all who contribute to the local rates (taxes) and exclude those who do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the principal duty of local bodies is imposition and expenditure of local taxation, those bearing the burden should have the franchise. Representation of minorities should follow the same rules as national representation, and plural voting based on money qualification is less objectionable for local bodies where money interest is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: One elective body per locality for all local business
rubrics_metrics.description: In each local circumscription there should be but one elective body to supervise all local business rather than separate elected bodies for different parts of that business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Division of labor pertains to execution (departments), not to control. A single superintending elected body can oversee various departments and ensure coherent policy, avoid waste and incoherent arrangements (as in London’s subdivision), and encourage participation of higher-calibre individuals who will not join piecemeal commissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local control should be organized by community of local interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Constituencies for local representation should be circumscribed on the principle of community of local interests so those with common interests can manage them together (e.g., each town should have one municipal council).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different kinds of local business require different representational areas; towns should not be subdivided into multiple municipal councils since quarters of the same town commonly share the same needs (paving, lighting, water, drainage, markets). Very small villages lacking distinct public character should be merged into larger circumscriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of a limited number of educated/ex officio members in some local bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain local institutions (example: Boards of Guardians) including a limited number of ex officio members such as justices of the peace (limited to a fraction, e.g., one third) brings educated perspectives and checks class interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex officio members secure the presence of a more educated class and act as a check on the self-interest of majority elected members. But this admixture is not universally justified (the author argues it is not justified for County Boards where the local business would attract country gentlemen to election).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local bodies should contain some of the best local minds
rubrics_metrics.description: Every local representative body should include a portion of the best minds of the locality to bring superior knowledge and ideas into contact with lower-grade members, thus raising the general political intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A school of civic education requires teachers as well as scholars: superior minds are unlikely to engage in piecemeal commissions but will serve on comprehensive local bodies. Their presence prevents degeneration into petty self-interest and provides useful instruction to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale local representation to suitability of population and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Very small villages that are not markedly distinct from surrounding rural districts should not claim separate municipal representation; local representation of rural districts should follow geographical and community-of-interest considerations (counties, provinces, agricultural/industrial districts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small places often lack a sufficient public to furnish a tolerable council and concentrate talent in one dominant individual; merging such places into larger circumscriptions yields better governance and avoids domination.
